newsitem.title: USA: Renowned U.S. trial lawyer Arthur Liman dies at age 65.
newsitem.headline: Renowned U.S. trial lawyer Arthur Liman dies at age 65.

text.p: Arthur Liman, a renowned trial lawyer who served as chief counsel to the Senate Iran-Contra Committee, died on Thursday after a long battle with cancer, his law firm announced. He was 64.
Liman, a senior partner with the international law firm of Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison, rose to prominence handling high-profile cases and clients.

In 1987, Liman was appointed chief counsel to the Senate committee investigating the Iran-Contra scandal in which White House aides in the Reagan administration secretly sold arms to Iran and diverted profits to Nicaragua's Contra rebels.

He was one of the lawyers who represented Michael Milken, Drexel Burnham Lambert's former junk bond chief who pleaded guilty in 1990 to six securities-related felonies and paid more than $1 billion in fines and restitution.

Liman also played a role in Pennzoil Co.'s legal battle with Texaco Inc. over Getty Oil Co., in which Pennzoil won a jury verdict of $11.1 billion, the largest civil lawsuit verdict in the United States.
Liman, who had been Pennzoil's attorney in New York during negotiations with Getty, served as a witness and adviser. The case was later settled for $3 billion.
Other clients included Henry Kissinger, entertainment firm Time Warner Inc., Polo/Ralph Lauren, Calvin Klein and food company H.J. Heinz Co.

"We are deeply saddened by the death of our partner," the firm said in a statement. "Arthur joined our firm 40 years ago. In those four decades, he established himself as one of the nation's leading lawyers, as a litigator and as a valued counsellor to corporate America, private citizens, government institutions and public officials."

A 1957 graduate of Yale Law School, Liman joined Paul, Weiss after graduation. He took a leave from the firm from 1961 to 1963 to work as an assistant U.S. attorney. He later served as chief counsel to the New York state commission that investigated the causes of the deadly 1971 uprising at Attica state prison.

Liman was president of New York City's Legal Aid Society from 1983 to 1985. He also served as chairman of New York's Capital Defender's Office, which is responsible for organising and providing defence for poor clients in capital cases.
He also served on the New York State Advisory Committee on Sentencing, appointed by then-Gov. Mario Cuomo to recommend revisions to the state's system for sentencing offenders.

Liman is survived by his wife Ellen, their three children Lewis, Douglas and Emily and a sister, Gladys. Lewis Liman is one of the prosecutors in the extortion trial of a woman claiming to be Bill Cosby's illegitimate daughter.
Funeral services for Liman will be held on Friday in New York City.
